title: Global cancer statistics 2022: GLOBOCAN estimates of incidence and mortality worldwide for 36 cancers in 185 countries
journal: CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians
key_finding: IARC GLOBOCAN 2022 estimates give close to 20 million new cancer cases and 9.7 million cancer deaths worldwide in 2022. Lung cancer was the most frequently diagnosed cancer (almost 2.5 million new cases, 12.4% of all cancers) and the leading cause of cancer death (about 1.8 million deaths, 18.7% of cancer deaths), ahead of female breast (11.6% of cases) and colorectal cancer (9.6% of cases; 9.3% of deaths). New cases are projected to reach 35 million by 2050 on demographic change alone.
use_for: Introduction: global lung cancer burden as the clinical motivation for chest CT AI
verified_how: Crossref record (metadata + abstract field)
flags: Published 2024 (allowed by task as the latest GLOBOCAN statistics paper). Publisher (Wiley) page not opened; numbers taken from the abstract deposited in Crossref.

title: Low-dose CT for lung cancer screening in a high-risk population (SUMMIT): a prospective, longitudinal cohort study
key_finding: Prospective London cohort (329 primary care practices) of 12,773 high-risk people aged 55-77 screened with low-dose CT; this report covers the baseline round. Lung cancer was diagnosed in 261 participants (2.0%), 79.3% at stage I or II and 77.0% treated by surgical resection; 12-month episode sensitivity was 97.0% and specificity 95.2% (false-positive rate 4.8%), with 11.6% of surgical resections benign. The authors conclude that large-scale LDCT screening can be delivered effectively to an ethnically and socioeconomically diverse population.
use_for: Introduction: recent prospective evidence that LDCT lung cancer screening works at scale (drives chest CT volume)
verified_how: Crossref record (metadata) + UCL Discovery repository record (abstract)
flags: Author list: Crossref gives 139 author entries (named writing group followed by SUMMIT consortium members, with repeats); the 36 names listed here are the first block before names start repeating and are taken to be the byline, published on behalf of the SUMMIT consortium - check against the journal PDF. Crossref shows an erratum (DOI 10.1016/S1470-2045(25)00204-9, May 2025) whose content I did not read. Online-first date not shown. Lancet website could not be opened. Funded by GRAIL.

title: Feasibility of AI as first reader in the 4-IN-THE-LUNG-RUN lung cancer screening trial: impact on negative-misclassifications and clinical referral rate
key_finding: On 3,678 baseline low-dose CT scans from the 4-IN-THE-LUNG-RUN trial, a commercial AI system (AVIEW-LCS) and radiologists read independently against an expert-panel reference. AI produced 31 negative misclassifications (0.8%) versus 407 (11.1%) for radiologists; used as first reader, AI would have missed 3 of 102 referrals (2.9%) compared with 12 of 102 (11.8%) for radiologists. The authors conclude AI is a feasible first reader to rule out negative baseline scans.
use_for: Clinical context: AI as an autonomous or first reader in CT screening, which raises the stakes for explanation and oversight
verified_how: Crossref record (metadata) + Erasmus University repository record (abstract)
flags: Crossref lists a corrigendum (DOI 10.1016/j.ejca.2025.115294, Eur J Cancer vol 218, March 2025); I could not read what it corrects, so re-check the numbers against the corrected version. ScienceDirect page not opened. Issue number not assigned (volume 216, article 115214).

title: Projected US Imaging Utilization, 2025 to 2055
journal: Journal of the American College of Radiology
key_finding: Using 2018-2022 claims (Medicare fee-for-service 5% sample plus the Inovalon database; 348,214,053 person-years), the authors project US imaging use to 2055. If current per-person use simply persists, 2055 utilisation is 16.9% to 26.9% above 2023 levels depending on modality; if recent trends continue to 2030 the range is 5.6% lower to 45.2% higher. Population growth explains 73-88% of the increase and ageing 12-27%.
use_for: Introduction: growth in imaging demand and radiologist workload as a driver for AI assistance
verified_how: Crossref record (metadata) + Ochsner institutional repository record (abstract)
flags: Covers all imaging modalities in the US, not chest CT specifically. Journal abbreviation 'J Am Coll Radiol' seen on the repository page (Crossref short title is the full name). Online-first date not shown. ScienceDirect page not opened.

title: External Test of a Deep Learning Algorithm for Pulmonary Nodule Malignancy Risk Stratification Using European Screening Data
key_finding: A nodule malignancy-risk deep learning model trained on NLST was tested retrospectively on pooled baseline scans from three European screening trials (DLCST, MILD, NELSON): 4,146 participants, 7,614 benign and 180 malignant nodules. AUCs were 0.98, 0.96 and 0.94 for cancers diagnosed within 1 year, 2 years and over the whole screening period, at least matching the PanCan model; for indeterminate 5-15 mm nodules, at 100% sensitivity for 1-year cancers, the model labelled 68.1% of benign cases low risk versus 47.4% for PanCan (a 39.4% relative reduction in false positives). On a size-matched subset the AUC was 0.79 versus 0.60.
use_for: Performance of deep learning on chest CT: large multi-trial external validation (2025)
verified_how: Crossref record + RSNA publisher page + UMC Utrecht repository record (abstract)
flags: Byline ends 'for the NELSON-POP consortium'; Crossref additionally lists the consortium members as authors (not included here). Retrospective design.

title: External Testing of a Deep Learning Model for Lung Cancer Risk from Low-Dose Chest CT
key_finding: The open-source Sybil lung-cancer-risk model was tested on 18,057 adults aged 50-80 from one Asian health-checkup centre (92 cancers over 6 years). Overall AUC was 0.91 for 1-year and 0.74 for 6-year risk; in heavy smokers the 1-year AUC for visible cancers was 0.94 and the 6-year AUC for future cancers 0.70, but in never- or light-smokers the AUC for future cancers fell to 0.56 (visible cancers 0.89). The model therefore transfers poorly to a population outside its training distribution for the task of predicting future cancer.
use_for: Generalisation limits of chest CT deep learning across populations (motivates transparency about where a model can be trusted)
verified_how: Crossref record + RSNA publisher page + Jeonbuk National University repository record (abstract)
flags: Single-centre retrospective external test; the generalisation gap is across population/smoking status rather than across scanners.

title: Artificial intelligence as an independent reader of risk-dominant lung nodules: influence of CT reconstruction parameters
key_finding: Baseline low-dose CT scans of 300 consecutive NELCIN-B3 screening participants (Tianjin) were read by a commercial AI system under four reconstruction settings, with two-radiologist consensus as reference. Per-scan sensitivity for a risk-dominant nodule was 77.5% with the medium-soft D45f/1 mm kernel but 31.5% with the sharp B80f/1 mm kernel (p<0.0001), and nodule-type agreement dropped from 87.7% to 17.7%, while the nodule detection rate itself (87.4% vs 82.0%) and a change from 1 mm to 2 mm slices made no significant difference. A single acquisition parameter can thus sharply change the output of a deployed AI reader.
use_for: Generalisation failure of commercial chest CT AI across reconstruction settings (2025-2026 evidence)
verified_how: Springer landing page (abstract) + Crossref record
flags: Issue year 2026 (vol 36, issue 3, March 2026); first online 29 Aug 2025. Two co-authors (Yu D, Yi J) are likely vendor-affiliated - affiliations not checked.

title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
key_finding: Consensus guideline from 117 experts in 50 countries setting out 30 best practices under six principles: fairness, universality, traceability, usability, robustness and explainability. Explainability has two recommendations: decide with end users and domain experts whether explanations are needed and define their goal, approach and limitations; and evaluate explanations both computationally for correctness and with end users for their effect on satisfaction, confidence and clinical performance. Traceability has six (risk management file, documentation, continuous quality control with calibrated uncertainty, periodic auditing and updating, AI logging, and governance with defined accountability).
use_for: Guidelines and regulation: current international consensus on what explainability and traceability require of clinical AI
verified_how: Crossref record + BMJ landing page (summary and recommendations) + BMJ correction notice
flags: A correction (BMJ 2025;388:r340, 17 Feb 2025) only fixes the spelling of a consortium member's name. The 49 named authors publish with the FUTURE-AI Consortium as a group; the exact wording of the group byline was not checked. Crossref gives no issue number.

title: TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models that use regression or machine learning methods
key_finding: Reporting guideline with a 27-item checklist (52 subitems) plus a 13-item abstract checklist for prediction-model studies using regression or machine learning; it supersedes TRIPOD 2015, which the authors say should no longer be used. Developed through a modified Delphi (200 respondents from 27 countries in round 2) and a consensus meeting, it adds explicit fairness items across sections, an open-science item (protocol, registration, data and code sharing) and a patient and public involvement item. It does not set a specific explainability requirement, noting only that machine learning models often cannot be reduced to a simple equation and so need fuller reporting.
use_for: Reporting standards for AI prediction models; shows that current reporting guidance stresses fairness and openness more than explanation
verified_how: Crossref record + BMJ landing page (abstract, summary points, methods)
flags: Published 2024 (current standard document, allowed by task). A correction notice dated 18 Apr 2024 (DOI 10.1136/bmj.q902) exists; its content was not read. Delphi participation figures come from the Methods section, not the abstract.

title: Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging (CLAIM): 2024 Update
key_finding: Delphi-based update of the CLAIM checklist by a panel of 73 recruited experts (72 completed both rounds), giving 44 items each answered Yes, No or Not Applicable. It replaces 'ground truth' with 'reference standard', discourages the bare word 'validation' in favour of 'internal testing' and 'external testing', deletes the old data-dictionary item and adds an item on image acquisition protocol. Item 31 asks authors to describe the methods used to explain or interpret model results, give their parameters and state how those methods were validated in the study.
use_for: Reporting standards for imaging AI: the specific CLAIM requirement to report and validate explainability methods
verified_how: Crossref record + RSNA publisher page (full special report)
flags: Published 2024 (current standard document, allowed by task). Byline is the seven named authors 'for the CLAIM 2024 Update Panel'; Crossref additionally lists the 72 panel members as authors (not included here). No abstract in Crossref; content read on the publisher page.

title: Guiding AI in radiology: ESR's recommendations for effective implementation of the European AI Act
key_finding: ESR AI Working Group statement on how the EU AI Act applies to imaging. Medical-device AI falls in the high-risk class; Article 13 obliges providers to give deployers clear instructions on intended purpose, performance, limitations and oversight measures, for which the ESR recommends model cards; Article 14 requires trained human oversight, with warnings about automation bias and deskilling; and under Article 26 any radiologist or department using AI clinically is a deployer who must follow instructions, supervise, monitor, keep logs and inform patients. The statement notes that methods and standards for transparency and explainability are still under development and asks the European Commission for sector-specific implementation guidance.
use_for: Regulation: EU AI Act transparency and human-oversight duties as read by European radiology
verified_how: Springer landing page (full statement) + Crossref record
flags: Article type is a society statement; the European Society of Radiology is listed as a group author.

authors: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency
title: Transparency for Machine Learning-Enabled Medical Devices: Guiding Principles
journal: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (web publication, Center for Devices and Radiological Health)
key_finding: Joint FDA, Health Canada and MHRA principles defining transparency as the degree to which appropriate information about a machine learning-enabled medical device (intended use, development, performance and, when available, logic) is clearly communicated to relevant audiences. 'Logic' is information on how an output was reached and 'explainability' is how well that logic can be understood by a person, so both are treated as aspects of transparency, to be provided 'when available' rather than as a stand-alone mandate. The principles are organised as who, why, what, where, when and how, and rest on human-centred design and on the 2021 good machine learning practice principles 7 and 9.
use_for: Regulation: how North American and UK regulators define transparency and explainability for ML devices
verified_how: FDA web page read in full
flags: Regulatory web document, not a journal article; no DOI, volume or pages. Date recorded is the page's 'content current as of' date (13 June 2024); the page metadata also carried an inconsistent later timestamp. Published 2024 (current standard document). Authorship is institutional.

title: Distinguishing between Rigor and Transparency in FDA Marketing Authorization of AI-enabled Medical Devices
key_finding: Special report separating validation rigour (quality of the evidence the FDA reviews) from validation transparency (how much of it the public can see). Of 1,247 AI marketing authorisations counted, 95.8% (1,195) went through the 510(k) pathway and 76.7% (956) were radiology devices; most radiology AI relies on retrospective standalone or reader studies, and no autonomous radiology AI device has yet been authorised. The authors recommend mandatory, checklist-based reporting of performance validation in 510(k) summaries, a public third-party performance database, reader studies for image-generating AI and prospective studies for future autonomous devices.
use_for: Regulation: limits of public transparency about FDA-cleared radiology AI
verified_how: Crossref record + RSNA publisher page (full text)
flags: Counts and percentages come from the article body rather than the short abstract. The paper addresses transparency of validation evidence, not model explainability as such.

title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement from the ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR & RSNA
key_finding: Joint statement of five radiology societies (USA, Canada, Europe, Australia and New Zealand) on evaluating, buying, deploying and monitoring radiology AI. It describes many deep learning systems as black boxes, says transparency about purpose, operating conditions, limitations and expected accuracy must be balanced against privacy, proprietary and security risks, and proposes that poor explainability be offset by a higher evidence bar (external or multi-centre data, prospective real-world evaluation). It also calls for local AI governance with periodic re-testing on local data (at least yearly) and drift monitoring, and warns of automation bias.
use_for: Multi-society position on transparency, explainability, monitoring and automation bias in radiology AI
verified_how: Springer landing page (full text, first 100,000 characters) + Crossref record
flags: Published 2024 (current standard document, allowed by task). The same statement was published in parallel in other society journals (search results showed versions in Radiology: Artificial Intelligence, Canadian Association of Radiologists Journal and Journal of Medical Imaging and Radiation Oncology); only the Insights into Imaging version was opened, so cite that one or verify the others separately. The final ~3% of the page text was not read.

title: On the practical, ethical, and legal necessity of clinical Artificial Intelligence explainability: an examination of key arguments
journal: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
key_finding: Systematized review of the arguments for and against requiring explainability in clinical AI. The authors conclude that fully autonomous black-box algorithms are persuasively ruled out on fundamental-rights and justice grounds, but that the published arguments do not establish a general explainability requirement for clinician-in-the-loop use, because lack of explanation does not by itself undermine clinicians' due diligence. They hold that trust should rest on transparency of development and sound clinical decision-making.
use_for: Debate on whether explainability should be a requirement for clinical AI (the 'against a blanket requirement' position)
verified_how: Springer landing page (abstract and conclusions) + Crossref record
flags: General clinical AI, not imaging-specific. The Springer page metadata listed only Veerapen but the byline and Crossref show both authors.

title: PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR): Checklist and Explanation
key_finding: Abstract not read (the publisher page did not render it). From the publisher page structure and the official PRISMA site: this is the reporting guideline for scoping reviews, with 20 essential and 2 optional reporting items; the two optional items concern critical appraisal of the sources of evidence, and five items of the original PRISMA list are marked not applicable. It was developed through an expert panel, Delphi survey rounds and an in-person meeting.
use_for: Methods: reporting standard followed by the review itself
verified_how: Crossref record (metadata) + ACP publisher page (headings and item structure) + PRISMA statement website (item counts) + EQUATOR Network entry
flags: Essential original (2018). The abstract text itself was not visible on any page I could open, so the item counts come from prisma-statement.org and the item structure from the article's explanation section; the size of the expert panel was not seen and is not stated here. PubMed and PMC were blocked by a browser check.

title: The PRISMA 2020 statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews
key_finding: Updated reporting guideline for systematic reviews that replaces the 2009 PRISMA statement. It provides a 27-item checklist in seven sections, an expanded checklist with detailed recommendations per item, an abstract checklist and revised flow diagrams for new and updated reviews, reflecting advances in how studies are identified, selected, appraised and synthesised.
use_for: Methods: source of the study-selection flow diagram used in the review
verified_how: Crossref record + BMJ landing page (abstract)
flags: Essential original (2021), optional per task. Volume 372 seen on bmj.com (Crossref record gives no volume). The BMJ page metadata lists a related 2026 item (DOI 10.1136/bmj-2026-100612) whose nature I did not check; it is not shown as a retraction or correction.

title: Fleischner Society: Glossary of Terms for Thoracic Imaging
key_finding: Fourth edition of the Fleischner Society consensus glossary, replacing the 1984, 1996 and 2008 versions. Terms were revised because some are new, some obsolete and others inconsistently used; related terms are grouped under thematic headings, signs and eponyms are reduced in favour of descriptive terms, each term is labelled as anatomy, physiology or pathology, and many more radiograph and CT images are included, with recommended usage given for controversial terms. Its stated aims include standardised communication, structured reporting and database searching.
use_for: Imaging vocabulary: authoritative term set a concept-based explanation layer for chest CT could draw on
verified_how: Crossref record + RSNA publisher page (abstract and introduction)
flags: Published 2024 (current standard document, allowed by task). The abstract gives no count of terms. Online-first date not shown (issue date February 2024).

title: ACR Lung-RADS v2022: Assessment Categories and Management Recommendations
key_finding: Citable article for the 2022 revision of the ACR Lung-RADS system for reporting and managing screen-detected lung nodules, tracing it from version 1.0 (2014) and 1.1 (2019). The v2022 changes add guidance on atypical pulmonary cysts, juxtapleural nodules, airway-centred nodules and findings that may be infectious, clarify how nodule growth is defined, and introduce stepped management for nodules that are stable or decreasing in size, with the supporting evidence and expert consensus summarised.
use_for: Imaging vocabulary: structured screening categories and descriptors that a concept layer could target
verified_how: Crossref records for both co-publications + MD Anderson repository record (abstract)
flags: Published 2024 (current standard document). Co-published with identical title and authors in Journal of the American College of Radiology 2024;21(3):473-488, DOI 10.1016/j.jacr.2023.09.009 (verified in Crossref); cite one version only. The abstract was read on the repository record for the Chest version. PubMed page was blocked by a browser check.

title: The Lung Image Database Consortium (LIDC) and Image Database Resource Initiative (IDRI): A Completed Reference Database of Lung Nodules on CT Scans
key_finding: Describes the public LIDC-IDRI database of 1,018 thoracic CT cases assembled by seven academic centres and eight imaging companies. Each scan was annotated by four experienced thoracic radiologists in two phases (blinded read, then unblinded review of all four sets of marks) using three categories: nodule 3 mm or larger, nodule smaller than 3 mm, and non-nodule 3 mm or larger. In total 7,371 lesions were marked as a nodule by at least one radiologist, 2,669 of them in the 3 mm-or-larger nodule category by at least one reader.
use_for: Imaging vocabulary and data: the reference dataset whose radiologist-rated nodule attributes underlie most concept-based chest CT XAI work
verified_how: Crossref record (metadata + abstract) + The Cancer Imaging Archive collection page (citation and dataset description)
flags: Essential original (2011). The three marking categories are taken from the TCIA collection page; the Crossref abstract supplied the counts. TCIA lists 1,010 subjects for what the paper describes as 1,018 cases. TCIA's citation omits the last author (Clarke LP) and has minor spelling variants; the Crossref spellings are used here. Wiley publisher page not opened.
